title: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Randomness lets discrete components produce continuous behavior

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Systems made of discrete components appear smooth and continuous on large scales mainly because microscopic randomness averages out the discreteness, and it does not matter whether that randomness comes from outside or from intrinsic generation, as shown by random walks, aggregation models and deterministic cellular automata that grow circular shapes.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 7: Mechanisms in Programs and Nature

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But it turns out that all that really seems to matter is that randomness is present: the mechanism through which it arises appears to be largely irrelevant.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 7, “Mechanisms in Programs and Nature”; section “The Phenomenon of Continuity” (from p. 327), p. 333. Scope: discrete systems such as random walks, aggregation models and cellular automata, and fluids made of molecules

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch07-12: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.76

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The computational examples can be reproduced and extended with standard simulation. Noise-source interventions have useful discriminating power for specified model classes. The broad extension to fluids and the assertion that averaging is the main cause remain only partially covered.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Simulate discrete growth and transport models with matched noise amplitudes supplied externally, pseudorandomly, or by deterministic chaotic rules, and measure anisotropy and interface roughness after coarse-graining. Convergence to the same smooth macroscopic observables would support mechanism-independence, while systematic source-dependent differences would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Smoothness, large scale, and mainly are model-dependent.

A finite model survey cannot establish the assertion for all discrete systems.

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim is pinned to three reproducible model classes, not to an open-ended survey of nature. Random-walk distributions are covered by the central limit theorem, and the aggregation and cellular-automaton comparisons are short simulations in public software. Removing randomness, or swapping its source, is a direct control, so the stated comparison can be confirmed or refuted now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Compare a roughness or circularity statistic for random walks, Eden-like aggregation, and deterministic cellular automata against the same models with the randomness removed. The central-limit case is already a theorem; the aggregation and cellular-automaton cases are finite simulations. Continuity collapsing when randomness is removed, and matching when intrinsic randomness replaces external noise, would support the claim; a systematic counterexample in these classes would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Smoothness needs an explicit statistic; visual roundness alone is not a decision criterion.

The Eden model still lacks a full proof, so that case is settled by simulation rather than by theorem.
